en.title: Environmental Management: the whole course
en.short: What environmental management covers, how the degree is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What environmental management is
sections.text:
Environmental management is the study of how people use, protect and repair the natural world, and how organisations decide what to do about air, water, land, waste, biodiversity and climate. It sits between science and policy. The science explains what is happening: how a pollutant moves through soil, how a river responds to waste. The policy side asks what should be done, who pays and who is affected.

Environmental problems are usually connected. A factory discharging into a river affects water quality, fish, farmers downstream and public health. Managing one part well can make another worse, so the course teaches systems thinking.

These summaries teach principles. They do not replace the law, standards or codes of any country. Environmental law, standards and professional registration differ between countries. Nigeria regulates through bodies such as NESREA and registers engineers through COREN; other countries have their own. Check the current official source.

sections.heading: How the degree is organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria a BSc usually takes four years; a polytechnic student may take an ND and then an HND. In the UK a BSc usually takes three years, and in Scotland often four. Ghana, Kenya and South Africa have their own patterns. A master’s usually takes one to two years and ends with a dissertation.

The early years are shared: ecology, chemistry, earth science, mathematics and statistics, economics, law and sustainable development. The middle years are the core of practice, from impact assessment to project management. Most courses end with a research project. A master’s adds governance, climate risk planning, modelling and research methods.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics build the base. Environmental science and systems thinking shows how parts connect. Ecology and biodiversity explain living systems. Environmental chemistry covers how pollutants react and move. Earth and climate science covers the atmosphere, oceans and climate. Mathematics and statistics give the tools to measure and test. Economics, law and sustainable development give the human and legal frame. Field methods and GIS teach how to collect and map data.

Core topics apply that base. Environmental impact assessment is the central planning tool. Management systems and auditing show how organisations control their own performance. Then come air quality, water resources and quality, wastewater and sanitation, soil and land degradation, and solid and hazardous waste with the circular economy. Climate mitigation and adaptation, and biodiversity conservation, deal with global change. Environmental health and toxicology, and risk assessment and industrial safety, deal with harm to people. Economics and valuation put money values on benefits. Policy and compliance, community engagement and environmental justice, and planning and project management cover how decisions are carried out. Professional ethics and research methods close the core.

At master’s level, governance, climate risk and adaptation planning, modelling and systems analysis, and dissertation research methods deepen the same themes.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn the science first, then the management. You cannot judge a policy on air pollution without knowing how pollutants disperse. Read each core topic beside its science topic.

Use the case method. Take a project, such as a new dam, landfill or factory in a named town, and work through it: what does it discharge, who is affected, what law applies, what would an impact assessment say, what monitoring would you require?

Practise the calculations: concentrations, loads, dilution, half-lives, cost-benefit. Write units on every line and check that answers are reasonable. Learn to read a regulation and find the part that applies. Keep a glossary of terms such as assimilative capacity, externality, mitigation hierarchy and due diligence.

sections.heading: Common mistakes

keyPoints: Environmental management links environmental science to policy, law and organisational decisions.
Problems are connected, so systems thinking matters more than isolated fixes.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Environmental law, standards and registration bodies differ by country; name the country and check the current source.
Learn the science behind each management topic, then practise the calculations with units.
Claims need evidence, and honest uncertainty is better than an invented figure.

en.title: Environmental science and systems thinking
en.short: Scope, systems thinking, biogeochemical cycles, carrying capacity, sustainability and indicators.

sections.heading: Scope and disciplines
sections.text: Environmental management is the work of guiding human activity and natural resources to reduce harm and reach agreed goals. It is multidisciplinary: environmental science supplies evidence; engineering designs controls; economics weighs costs and benefits; law and policy set rules; social sciences explain behaviour and questions of fairness. A manager therefore works with specialists rather than alone. The field ranges from local waste and water problems to national and global issues.

sections.heading: Systems thinking
sections.text: A system is a set of connected parts whose behaviour comes from their interactions. Systems thinking studies stocks (amounts stored), flows (rates of change), feedback loops (reinforcing or balancing), delays, resilience (ability to absorb change and recover) and thresholds (points where a system shifts to a different state). A change in one part can cause effects elsewhere or later. For example, cutting trees changes water flow, soil loss and local income.

sections.heading: Cycles and limits
sections.text: Biogeochemical cycles move water and elements such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus between atmosphere, land, water and living things. Reservoirs store them; fluxes move them. Human actions such as burning fossil fuels and applying fertiliser alter these fluxes. Carrying capacity is the maximum population or load an environment can support indefinitely under given conditions without degradation. It is not fixed: technology, consumption, trade and time change it. In a made-up lake, a sustainable fish yield of 12,000 kg a year supports 12,000 ÷ 60 = 200 people if each needs 60 kg; at 80 kg each it supports 150. Other resources also matter.

sections.heading: Sustainability and indicators
sections.text: Sustainability means meeting present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs. It has environmental, social and economic dimensions, so a solution that harms one dimension is weak. Environmental indicators are measured variables that show condition or trend, such as forest cover, fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentration or access to safe water. They need clear units, a baseline and careful interpretation, because one indicator rarely tells the whole story.

keyPoints: Environmental management is multidisciplinary, drawing on science, engineering, economics, law and social sciences.
Systems thinking studies stocks, flows, feedbacks, delays, resilience and thresholds.
Biogeochemical cycles move water and elements between reservoirs; human activity changes fluxes.
Carrying capacity is the maximum load an environment can support indefinitely under given conditions; it is not fixed.
Simplified supportable number = sustainable supply ÷ demand per person.
Environmental indicators need units, baselines and careful interpretation.

en.title: Ecology and Biodiversity Foundations
en.short: Populations, communities, ecosystems, succession, trophic levels, nutrient cycling, biodiversity and ecosystem services.

sections.heading: Populations and communities
sections.text:
A population is a group of individuals of one species living in the same area at the same time. Its size changes through births, deaths, immigration and emigration. A community is all the populations of different species that interact in that area. Species compete, eat one another and share habitats.

A community plus its non-living surroundings, such as soil, water, air and climate, forms an ecosystem. Ecologists study these levels because a change at one level can affect the others.

sections.heading: Ecosystems and energy
sections.text:
Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight captured by producers, mainly plants and algae. Herbivores are primary consumers, carnivores are secondary or tertiary consumers, and decomposers break down dead matter. Each step is a trophic level. Energy is lost as heat and used in life processes, so fewer individuals usually live at higher levels.

Nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycle between organisms and the environment. Decomposers return nutrients to soil and water, making them available again.

sections.heading: Succession and disturbance
sections.text:
Succession is the gradual change in species composition over time. Primary succession starts on bare rock or new volcanic land with no soil. Secondary succession starts where soil remains after fire, flood or farming. Pioneer species arrive first; later species replace them as conditions change.

Disturbance is any event that removes organisms or alters resources, such as fire, storm, grazing or logging. Moderate disturbance can sometimes maintain variety; severe or frequent disturbance can degrade an ecosystem.

sections.heading: Biodiversity and services
sections.text:
Biodiversity has three common levels: genetic diversity within a species, species diversity in a community, and ecosystem diversity across a landscape. Ecosystem services are the benefits people obtain from ecosystems. They include provisioning services such as food and timber, regulating services such as flood control and pollination, supporting services such as soil formation, and cultural services such as recreation.

In a made-up case, Amina and Chidi farm near a river. Keeping a strip of trees reduces erosion and shelters bees that pollinate their crops.

keyPoints: Populations are groups of one species; communities are interacting populations of different species.
An ecosystem is a community plus its non-living environment, linked by energy flow and nutrient cycling.
Energy enters ecosystems through producers and is lost as heat along trophic levels.
Succession is directional change in species over time; disturbance can reset or maintain it.
Biodiversity has genetic, species and ecosystem levels.
Ecosystem services are the benefits ecosystems provide to people, such as food, flood control and pollination.

en.title: Environmental Chemistry: Matter, pH and Pollutant Fate
en.short: Matter and units, pH, solubility, partitioning, redox, nutrients, metals, pollutants, fate and bioavailability.

sections.heading: Matter, units and pH
sections.text:
Environmental chemistry studies substances in air, water, soil and organisms. Matter is atoms and molecules. Amounts use moles (mol); concentration uses molarity (mol/L) or mass concentration (mg/L). In dilute water, 1 mg/L is about 1 part per million (ppm).

pH = −log10[H+], where [H+] is hydrogen ion concentration in mol/L. At 25 °C pure water has pH 7. Example: [H+] = 1 × 10−5 mol/L gives pH = −log10(1 × 10−5) = 5, so acidic. pH affects reaction rates and metal solubility.

sections.heading: Solubility and partitioning
sections.text:
Solubility is the maximum amount of a substance that dissolves in a solvent at a stated temperature. It limits how much pollutant can move in water.

Partitioning is distribution between two phases. The solid-water partition coefficient is Kd = concentration in solid ÷ concentration in water at equilibrium, often in L/kg. The octanol-water coefficient Kow compares preference for fat-like octanol against water; high Kow suggests accumulation in organisms and soils. Use measured values.

sections.heading: Redox, nutrients and metals
sections.text:
Redox reactions transfer electrons: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain. Redox potential, Eh (volts) or pe, shows whether conditions are oxidising or reducing.

Nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus are essential but excess can cause eutrophication, excessive plant growth that depletes oxygen. Metals occur in different chemical forms (species), and toxicity depends on the species, not only total concentration. Dissolved mercury and methylmercury are more hazardous than many solid forms. Some metals are essential at low doses but toxic above a threshold.

sections.heading: Pollutants, fate and bioavailability
sections.text:
Organic pollutants include fuels, solvents, pesticides and persistent organic pollutants (POPs). Many are hydrophobic, so they sorb to soil and sediment or bioaccumulate.

Fate and transport describe movement and change: advection with flowing water or air, dispersion, sorption, volatilisation and degradation. Bioavailability is the fraction of a substance that organisms can take up. It depends on speciation, solubility, sorption and route of exposure. A metal may be present in soil but unavailable if tightly bound. Risk therefore depends on bioavailable concentration, not only total amount.

keyPoints: pH = −log10[H+], with [H+] in mol/L; at 25 °C pure water has pH 7.
In dilute water, 1 mg/L is about 1 ppm; concentration can be molarity (mol/L) or mass concentration (mg/L).
Kd = concentration in solid ÷ concentration in water at equilibrium, and high Kow suggests accumulation in organisms and soils.
Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain; Eh or pe indicates oxidising or reducing conditions.
Excess nitrogen and phosphorus can cause eutrophication, and metal toxicity depends on the chemical species.
Fate and transport include advection, dispersion, sorption, volatilisation and degradation, while bioavailability is the fraction organisms can take up.

en.title: Earth and Climate Science
en.short: Earth’s spheres, energy balance, greenhouse effect, natural variability and evidence for climate change.

sections.heading: Four spheres
sections.text:
Earth science treats the planet as four linked systems. The atmosphere is the gas layer held by gravity. The hydrosphere is all water on and near the surface: oceans, lakes, rivers, groundwater and ice.

The lithosphere is the rigid outer rock shell, including the crust and uppermost mantle. The biosphere is all living things and the parts of other spheres they use. Matter and energy move between them, so a change in one can affect the others.

sections.heading: Energy balance
sections.text:
The Sun is Earth’s main energy source. Sunlight arrives as shortwave radiation. The fraction reflected back to space is the albedo. The rest is absorbed and later leaves as longwave infrared radiation.

In balance, absorbed solar energy equals outgoing infrared energy. A global average uses the solar constant S, about 1361 W/m². Earth intercepts sunlight over a disc of area πR² but radiates over a sphere of area 4πR². With albedo 0.30: average absorbed = S(1 − 0.30) ÷ 4 = 1361 × 0.70 ÷ 4 = 238 W/m². This is a global average, not a local value.

sections.heading: Greenhouse effect and evidence
sections.text:
Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane and nitrous oxide absorb some outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back to the surface. This natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warmer than it would be without an atmosphere; human emissions enhance it.

Climate also varies naturally: El Niño and La Niña shift ocean and air patterns, large volcanic eruptions can cool the surface briefly, and orbital changes act over tens of thousands of years. Climate is the long-term pattern of weather, usually averaged over 30 years.

Evidence for recent change comes from many independent records: thermometers, satellites, ice cores, tree rings and sediments. They show rising global temperature and ocean heat, shrinking ice and rising sea level. The lower atmosphere warming while the upper atmosphere cools fits greenhouse warming, not a stronger Sun. Long records and multiple lines of evidence matter, not one cold year.

keyPoints: Earth’s four spheres are the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere, linked by flows of matter and energy.
In energy balance, absorbed solar energy equals outgoing infrared energy; average absorbed = S(1 − albedo) ÷ 4.
With S = 1361 W/m² and albedo 0.30, average absorbed is about 238 W/m².
Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, warming the surface; human emissions enhance this natural effect.
Natural variability includes El Niño and La Niña, volcanic eruptions and orbital cycles, and it sits on top of human influence.
Evidence for climate change comes from many independent records, not a single weather event.

en.title: Environmental Mathematics and Statistics
en.short: Units, concentrations, mass balance, residence time, rates, statistics, sampling and hypothesis tests.

sections.heading: Units and concentrations
sections.text:
SI units are the base. Prefixes change units by powers of ten: 1 mg = 10⁻³ g and 1 m³ = 1,000 L. To convert, multiply by a factor that cancels the old unit. Concentration is amount of substance per stated volume or mass. For water, 1 mg/L = 1 g/m³ and is about 1 part per million (ppm), since 1 L of water has mass near 1 kg. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass; molarity = moles ÷ litres.

Example: 25 mg/L = 25 × (1 g ÷ 1,000 mg) × (1,000 L ÷ 1 m³) = 25 g/m³.

sections.heading: Mass balance, residence time
sections.text:
A mass balance accounts for matter entering, leaving and accumulating in a control volume. Accumulation = input − output. At steady state, accumulation is zero, so input = output for a conservative substance with no reaction. Residence time τ is average time in the system: τ = mass in system ÷ flow rate, or volume ÷ flow for water.

Example: a lake holds 2.0 × 10⁶ m³ and outflow is 5,000 m³/day. τ = 2,000,000 ÷ 5,000 = 400 days.

sections.heading: Rates and statistics
sections.text:
A rate is change ÷ time; flux is mass per area per time. Descriptive statistics summarise data. Mean = Σx ÷ n. Median = middle ordered value. Sample standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)) measures spread.

Example: a load of 12 kg/day falls on 0.5 ha. Flux = 12 ÷ 0.5 = 24 kg/ha/day.

sections.heading: Sampling and testing
sections.text: A sample must represent the population. Random sampling gives every unit an equal chance of selection; stratified sampling divides the population into groups first. Measurements carry uncertainty from instruments, sampling and natural variation. Report units, significant figures and an uncertainty range. In a hypothesis test, state a null hypothesis H0 and alternative H1, choose significance level α, and calculate a p-value. Reject H0 if p < α. A t-test compares means. Statistical significance is not the same as practical importance.

keyPoints: Convert units by multiplying by a factor that cancels the old unit; 1 mg/L = 1 g/m³ and is about 1 ppm in water.
Concentration = mass ÷ volume; moles = mass ÷ molar mass; molarity = moles ÷ litres.
Mass balance: accumulation = input − output; at steady state input = output for a conservative substance.
Residence time τ = mass in system ÷ flow rate, or volume ÷ flow for water.
Rate = change ÷ time; flux = mass ÷ (area × time). Mean = Σx ÷ n; sample standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)).
In a hypothesis test, reject H0 when p < α, but check sampling, uncertainty and practical importance before drawing conclusions.

en.title: Principles of Environmental Economics
en.short: Scarcity, opportunity cost, externalities, public goods, commons, market failure and cost-benefit reasoning.

sections.heading: Scarcity and choice
sections.text: Environmental resources are limited compared with human wants. This scarcity forces choices: land kept as forest cannot also be farmed, and water used for irrigation cannot be left in a river. Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up. If the forgone farm profit is 400,000, that amount is part of the opportunity cost of conserving the forest. Environmental protection is therefore not free, even when no money changes hands.

sections.heading: Externalities and commons
sections.text: An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on a third party and is not reflected in the price. Pollution from a factory is a negative externality; a farmer’s bees pollinating a neighbour’s crop can be a positive one. A public good is non-rival and non-excludable: one person’s use does not reduce another’s, and no one can easily be stopped from using it. Climate stability is often treated as a public good. A common pool resource is rival but non-excludable, such as a fish stock or shared groundwater. Each user gains from taking more, while the cost is shared, so the resource can be overused. This is one form of market failure, where prices fail to signal true social costs and benefits.

sections.heading: Cost-benefit reasoning
sections.text: Cost-benefit reasoning compares the gains and losses of a choice. Net benefit is total benefits minus total costs. A project is worth doing if its net benefit is positive and is larger than the best alternative’s net benefit. Suppose a town can fund one project. Wetland restoration costs 2,000,000 and gives benefits of 3,200,000, so net benefit is 3,200,000 − 2,000,000 = 1,200,000. A car park costs 2,000,000 and gives benefits of 2,500,000, so net benefit is 500,000. Restoration is preferred. Its opportunity cost is the forgone car park net benefit of 500,000. When benefits arrive in future years, discount them: present value = future value ÷ (1 + r)^t, where r is the discount rate and t is the number of years. At r = 10% and t = 2, 1,210,000 ÷ 1.1² = 1,000,000.

keyPoints: Scarcity means environmental resources are limited relative to wants, so every use has an opportunity cost.
Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone.
An externality is a third-party cost or benefit not reflected in prices.
Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable; common pool resources are rival but non-excludable and can be overused.
Market failure occurs when prices do not reflect true social costs and benefits.
Net benefit = total benefits − total costs; present value = future value ÷ (1 + r)^t; choose the option with the highest positive net benefit.

en.title: Principles of Environmental Law and Policy
en.short: Sources of environmental law, key principles and the link between treaties and national law.

sections.heading: Sources of environmental law
sections.text: Environmental law has several sources. A constitution may give a right to a healthy environment, as South Africa’s does. Statutes create agencies and duties; Nigeria’s NESREA Act 2007 is one example. Regulations and permits add detail. Case law, including nuisance, also applies, and customary rules can govern land and water. International treaties bind states that ratify them, but often need national legislation before domestic courts apply them. Declarations are not binding.

sections.heading: Key principles
sections.text: Four key principles guide policy. Prevention stops harm before it happens, through permits and planning. Precaution applies when science is uncertain: serious or irreversible harm is possible, so cost-effective action is not postponed. Polluter pays means the polluter bears the cost of control and cleanup. Public participation means affected people can get information, comment on decisions and seek review. South Africa’s National Environmental Management Act 1998 lists these principles. Nigeria’s NESREA Act 2007 also provides for enforcement, but details differ.

sections.heading: International and national law
sections.text: International agreements are made between states. Treaties and conventions, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity 1992, bind parties. The Paris Agreement 2015 is a treaty on climate. A state usually implements a treaty through its own laws. National law is binding inside the country and is enforced by regulators and courts. A treaty may guide policy, but a factory’s discharge limit comes from a national permit or regulation. The Rio Declaration 1992 is a declaration, not a binding treaty, though it shaped many national laws.

sections.heading: Worked case
sections.text: A made-up tannery in Kano, Nigeria, discharges effluent into a stream. Prevention: the regulator sets permit conditions before discharge. Precaution: it requires monitoring for chromium while evidence is incomplete. Polluter pays: the tannery pays for treatment and cleanup. Public participation: downstream residents see monitoring reports and comment on the permit. If Nigeria has ratified a relevant treaty, the treaty still needs Nigerian law to be enforced in court. Check current NESREA regulations and Nigerian law for exact duties and penalties.

keyPoints: Environmental law comes from constitutions, statutes, regulations, case law, customary rules and international treaties.
Prevention stops harm early; precaution allows action when scientific evidence is uncertain.
Polluter pays places control and cleanup costs on the polluter; public participation gives affected people information, voice and review.
International treaties bind states that ratify them, while national law binds people and organisations inside a country.
A treaty often needs national legislation before domestic courts can enforce it; declarations are not binding law.
South Africa’s NEMA 1998 and Nigeria’s NESREA Act 2007 are country-specific examples; check the current text for exact duties and penalties.

en.title: Sustainable Development
en.short: Brundtland definition, equity, SDGs, indicators, decoupling and growth limits.

sections.heading: Definition and equity
sections.text: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. This is the Brundtland definition, from Our Common Future (1987), the report of the World Commission on Environment and Development. It joins environmental protection with social and economic goals. Intergenerational equity is the fairness claim inside it: future people should inherit a fair share of natural, human and produced capital. Intra-generational equity, fairness within the present generation, is also implied but stated less clearly. Critics call the definition vague: 'needs’ and 'compromising' are not defined, and it can be used to justify continued growth.

sections.heading: Goals and indicators
sections.text: The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are 17 goals adopted by UN member states in 2015 as part of the 2030 Agenda. They cover poverty, health, education, water, energy, cities, climate, biodiversity and partnerships. Indicators are measures used to track progress, such as GDP per person, the Human Development Index, ecological footprint and the SDG indicator framework. No single indicator captures sustainability, because it has environmental, social and economic dimensions. A made-up district, Okoro, reports rising income but falling groundwater and school attendance; that pattern shows why several indicators are read together.

sections.heading: Decoupling and limits
sections.text: Decoupling means breaking the link between economic growth and environmental pressure. Relative decoupling occurs when pressure per unit of GDP falls while total pressure still rises. Absolute decoupling occurs when total pressure falls as the economy grows. Evidence is mixed and depends on the pressure and country. The growth-versus-limits debate sets green growth and circular economy claims against ecological economics, which argues that a finite planet cannot support endless material growth and proposes a steady-state economy, one held at a stable level of material and energy use. Others stress innovation and dematerialisation, using less material per unit of output. The Brundtland idea does not settle this debate; it leaves room for both.

keyPoints: Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising future generations’ ability to meet their own needs.
Intergenerational equity requires a fair share of natural, human and produced capital to be passed to future people.
The SDGs are 17 UN goals adopted in 2015 under the 2030 Agenda.
Indicators track environmental, social and economic dimensions; no single indicator is enough.
Relative decoupling lowers pressure per unit of GDP; absolute decoupling lowers total pressure.
The growth-versus-limits debate is unresolved, with green growth and steady-state economics offering different answers.

en.title: Field Methods, Maps and GIS
en.short: Sampling, field records, map scale, GIS layers, remote sensing, GPS and data quality.

sections.heading: Sampling and records
sections.text:
Sampling design is the plan for choosing where and how much to measure. The population is all items of interest; a sample is the part studied. Random sampling gives every unit an equal chance of selection. Stratified sampling divides the area into strata (subgroups), such as land-use types, and samples each. Systematic sampling uses a regular grid. Sample size depends on variability and precision needed.

Field measurement must be repeatable. Calibrate instruments, record units, method, time, location and observer, and take replicates and blanks (target-free samples). Chain of custody is the written record of a sample from collection to laboratory, with dates, signatures and transfers.

sections.heading: Maps and scale
sections.text:
A map is a scaled drawing of part of the earth on a flat surface. It needs a scale, legend, north arrow and projection. Projection is the method for representing the curved earth on a plane; every projection distorts shape, area, distance or direction. Scale is the ratio of map distance to ground distance.

Example: on a 1:50,000 map, 4 cm equals 4 × 50,000 = 200,000 cm = 2,000 m = 2 km.

sections.heading: GIS and remote sensing
sections.text:
A GIS (geographic information system) stores, displays and analyses spatial data. A GIS layer is one theme of data, such as roads or rivers. Vector layers use points, lines and polygons; raster layers use grid cells. Overlay combines layers to find relationships.

Remote sensing measures reflected or emitted energy from aircraft or satellites. Resolution matters: spatial (pixel size), spectral (wavelength bands), temporal (revisit time) and radiometric (number of brightness levels).

sections.heading: GPS and data quality
sections.text:
GPS is one of several global navigation satellite systems (GNSS). A receiver calculates position from satellites. Accuracy varies with satellite geometry, buildings, trees and correction services. Record the coordinate reference system and datum (reference frame), because coordinates can mean different places under different datums.

Data quality includes accuracy (closeness to the true value), precision (repeatability), completeness, consistency and timeliness. Keep metadata: source, date, method and processing. Check positions against independent points.

keyPoints: Sampling design states how units are chosen; random, stratified and systematic designs are common.
Calibrate instruments, record metadata and keep a signed chain of custody for samples.
Map scale is map distance ÷ ground distance; on a 1:50,000 map, 4 cm equals 2 km.
GIS layers are vector or raster themes; overlay combines them.
Remote sensing resolution is spatial, spectral, temporal and radiometric.
Data quality means accuracy, precision, completeness, consistency and timeliness; record the datum with GPS coordinates.

en.title: Environmental Impact Assessment
en.short: Screening, scoping, baseline, prediction, significance, mitigation, the EMP, review, decision and public participation.

sections.heading: Screening and scoping
sections.text: Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is a formal process for predicting the environmental and social effects of a proposed project before a decision is made. Screening decides whether an EIA is required. It uses project lists or thresholds such as size, location and likely emissions. These differ by country, so check the national law. Scoping decides which issues, alternatives and boundaries the EIA will study. It produces terms of reference and identifies stakeholders. Public participation should begin here, because affected people can name concerns that outsiders miss.

sections.heading: Baseline and prediction
sections.text: The baseline describes the environment before the project: air, water, soil, ecology, land use, health and livelihoods. Good baseline data are recent, local and matched to predicted impacts. Impact prediction estimates how the project will change those conditions. It states magnitude, spatial extent, duration, frequency and probability. Methods include checklists, interaction matrices, modelling and expert judgement. Significance is the judgement of how much an impact matters. It compares the predicted change with the baseline and with receptors such as people, ecosystems and protected areas. There is no single universal formula; criteria and thresholds vary by country and decision context.

sections.heading: Mitigation and decision
sections.text: Mitigation follows a hierarchy: avoid, minimise, restore, then offset residual harm. The environmental management plan (EMP) turns mitigation into actions, with responsibilities, timing, monitoring indicators, reporting and a budget. Review checks the report for completeness and quality. The decision may be approval, approval with conditions, or refusal. Public participation runs from scoping through review and decision. Legal requirements differ by country; Nigeria’s Environmental Impact Assessment Act 1992 is one example. Check the official source. Case: a proposed quarry near a river in Ogun State, Nigeria. Screening likely triggers EIA; scoping names dust, noise and river sediment; baseline measures air, stream flow and downstream water use; prediction finds high significance for water users; mitigation uses water sprays, settling ponds and a buffer; the EMP assigns monitoring; the authority decides with public input.

keyPoints: Screening decides whether an EIA is needed; project lists and thresholds differ by country.
Scoping sets the issues, boundaries, alternatives and stakeholders for the study.
Baseline data describe pre-project conditions; impact prediction estimates magnitude, extent, duration and probability.
Significance compares predicted change with the baseline and with receptors; no universal formula exists.
Mitigation follows avoid, minimise, restore, offset; the EMP sets actions, responsibilities, monitoring and reporting.
Review and decision can approve, impose conditions or refuse; public participation should run throughout, and legal requirements differ by country.

en.title: Environmental Management Systems and Auditing
en.short: ISO 14001, aspects and impacts, objectives, operational control, auditing and certification.

sections.heading: The EMS and ISO 14001
sections.text: An environmental management system (EMS) is the set of policies, plans, procedures, responsibilities and records an organisation uses to manage its environmental effects. ISO 14001 is the best-known international standard for an EMS; the current version is ISO 14001:2015. It can be used by any organisation, public or private, and it is voluntary. The standard requires a commitment to meet applicable legal and other requirements, but it does not set universal pollution limits. Those limits come from national law, permits and local rules, which differ by country.

sections.heading: Aspects, impacts and planning
sections.text: Planning starts with environmental aspects and impacts. An aspect is an element of an activity, product or service that interacts or can interact with the environment, such as fuel storage at a workshop. An impact is the resulting change, such as soil contamination after a leak. The organisation decides which aspects are significant and sets environmental objectives, which are results to be achieved and should be measurable where practicable. Documentation records the policy, roles, aspects, objectives and procedures. Operational control means setting work instructions, training and checks so that significant aspects are managed in daily work.

sections.heading: Check, act and certify
sections.text: ISO 14001 uses the plan-do-check-act cycle. Plan sets aspects, objectives and controls. Do implements them. Check monitors, measures and audits. Act corrects problems and improves the system. An audit is a systematic, independent and documented check against criteria. Internal audits are done by the organisation; certification audits are done by an external certification body, usually accredited by a national accreditation body. Certification confirms the EMS meets ISO 14001, not that the organisation has zero impact. Continual improvement means repeated small or large gains over time, not a single certificate.

keyPoints: ISO 14001 is a voluntary international standard for an environmental management system; the current version is ISO 14001:2015.
An environmental aspect is an element of an activity, product or service that can interact with the environment; an impact is the resulting change.
The EMS follows plan-do-check-act: plan aspects, objectives and controls; do them; check by monitoring and audit; act to improve.
Significant aspects are managed through documentation, operational control, training and work instructions.
Internal audits check the EMS against criteria; certification is an external audit and does not guarantee zero environmental impact.
Legal limits differ by country; ISO 14001 requires compliance but does not set the limits.

en.title: Air Quality Management: Sources, Dispersion and Control
en.short: Pollutant sources, dispersion, monitoring, country standards, control technologies and indoor air plans.

sections.heading: Sources and pollutants
sections.text: Air pollutants are substances in air that harm health, ecosystems or materials. Primary pollutants are emitted directly, such as particulate matter (PM), sulphur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen oxides (NOx), carbon monoxide (CO) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Secondary pollutants form in the air, such as ozone and secondary PM. Sources include point sources (factory stacks), area sources (open burning, dust), mobile sources (vehicles) and natural sources (wind-blown dust, wildfires). Indoor sources include cooking smoke, tobacco smoke and some building materials.

sections.heading: Dispersion and monitoring
sections.text: Dispersion is how pollutants spread and dilute. It depends on wind speed, atmospheric stability, stack height and terrain. A box model gives C = Q ÷ (u H W), where Q is emission rate, u is wind speed, H is mixing height and W is width. Example: Q = 10 g/s, u = 2 m/s, H = 100 m, W = 1,000 m gives C = 10 ÷ (2 × 100 × 1,000) = 0.00005 g/m³ = 50 µg/m³. Monitoring combines fixed monitors, passive samplers and calibrated low-cost sensors with emission inventories and models.

sections.heading: Standards and control
sections.text: Air quality standards differ by country. The World Health Organization (WHO) publishes health-based air quality guidelines, but they are not law. Countries set enforceable limits, for example the US National Ambient Air Quality Standards under the Clean Air Act, EU ambient air quality directives, and national regulations enforced by NESREA in Nigeria. Check current official limits. Control technologies include cyclones, fabric filters, electrostatic precipitators and wet scrubbers for particles; absorption, adsorption, catalytic converters and low-NOx burners for gases; and cleaner fuels, inspection and maintenance, and public transport for vehicles.

sections.heading: Indoor air and plans
sections.text: Indoor air quality is affected by cooking smoke, tobacco smoke, dampness and building materials. Radon, a radioactive gas, varies with geology. Control relies on source removal, ventilation and improved stoves. An air quality management plan sets objectives, inventories emissions, monitors air, models hotspots, applies controls, enforces rules and informs the public. Review when data and standards change.

keyPoints: Primary pollutants are emitted directly; secondary pollutants form in the air, such as ozone and secondary particulate matter.
Dispersion depends on wind speed, atmospheric stability, stack height and terrain.
Box model: C = Q ÷ (u H W), with Q in g/s, u in m/s, H and W in m, giving g/m³.
Air quality standards are legal limits that differ by country; WHO guidelines are health-based advice, not law.
Control technologies remove particles with cyclones, filters, precipitators or scrubbers, and gases with absorption, adsorption, catalysis or low-NOx burners.
Indoor air management prioritises source control and ventilation, and an air quality management plan combines inventory, monitoring, modelling, controls, enforcement and public information.

en.title: Water Resources and Water Quality Management
en.short: Catchment water balance, demand, water quality, pollution, monitoring, treatment and catchment protection.

sections.heading: Catchment water balance
sections.text:
A catchment is the land area draining to a common outlet. Its water balance over a period is P = ET + Q + ΔS, where P is precipitation, ET is evapotranspiration (water lost by evaporation and plant transpiration), Q is runoff and ΔS is change in storage in soil, groundwater or lakes. Use the same units, usually millimetres of depth.

Example: a 50 km² catchment receives 1,200 mm of rain. ET is 800 mm and storage rises by 100 mm. Then Q = 1,200 − 800 − 100 = 300 mm. Volume = 0.3 m × 50,000,000 m² = 15,000,000 m³.

sections.heading: Demand and allocation
sections.text: Demand comes from domestic, agricultural, industrial and environmental uses. Allocation sets who may take water, how much and when, often through permits or water rights. Priorities and environmental flows (water left in rivers for ecosystems) differ by country. Check the national water law and regulator. Reducing leaks and improving efficiency stretch existing supply.

sections.heading: Quality and pollution
sections.text: Water quality parameters are physical (turbidity, colour), chemical (pH, nitrate, metals) and biological (faecal indicator bacteria such as E. coli, which signal faecal contamination). Pollution sources are point (a factory outfall or sewer pipe) or diffuse (farm runoff, urban stormwater). Pathogens and nutrients are common concerns. Standards and guidelines differ by country and use; check the current national standard or WHO guidelines.

sections.heading: Monitoring, treatment, protection
sections.text: Monitoring uses representative sampling, preserved samples and accredited laboratories; frequency depends on risk and regulation. Drinking-water treatment commonly follows coagulation and flocculation (clumping particles), sedimentation, filtration and disinfection. Catchment protection controls land use, sanitation and buffer zones around sources. Treatment alone is not enough; protect the source.

keyPoints: Catchment water balance: P = ET + Q + ΔS; keep units consistent.
Allocation decides who takes water and how much; rules differ by country.
Water quality is described by physical, chemical and biological parameters.
Pollution sources are point or diffuse; diffuse sources are harder to control.
Drinking-water treatment: coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, disinfection.
Protect catchments through land-use control, sanitation and buffer zones.

en.title: Wastewater and Sanitation Management
en.short: Domestic and industrial wastewater, treatment stages, sludge, reuse and sanitation.

sections.heading: Sources and strength
sections.text:
Wastewater is water used and carrying pollutants. Domestic wastewater includes blackwater from toilets and greywater from sinks, baths and laundry. Industrial wastewater varies; factories may need pre-treatment before discharge to a sewer or river.

Strength is described by biochemical oxygen demand (BOD, oxygen used by microbes to break down organic matter), chemical oxygen demand (COD), suspended solids, nutrients and pathogens. High-strength industrial waste can upset biological treatment, so segregation and pre-treatment matter.

sections.heading: Treatment stages
sections.text:
Primary treatment is physical: screening, grit removal and sedimentation. Settled solids form primary sludge. Secondary treatment is biological: microbes convert dissolved organic matter into cells and carbon dioxide. Common systems are activated sludge, trickling filters and waste stabilisation ponds. Tertiary treatment polishes effluent by removing nutrients, filtering particles or disinfecting with chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.

Example: flow 2,000 m³/day, influent BOD 250 mg/L, effluent BOD 20 mg/L. Since 1 mg/L = 0.001 kg/m³, influent load = 2,000 × 0.250 = 500 kg/day; effluent load = 2,000 × 0.020 = 40 kg/day. Removal = (500 − 40) ÷ 500 × 100 = 92%.

sections.heading: Sludge and reuse
sections.text: Sludge is the solids and microbial growth removed from the process. It is thickened, stabilised by anaerobic or aerobic digestion, dewatered and then used or disposed of. Treated sludge may become biosolids for land application if contaminant limits are met. Reusing treated wastewater for irrigation, industry or aquifer recharge can save water, but quality must match the use and protect health.

sections.heading: Sanitation and standards
sections.text: Sanitation systems include on-site latrines and septic tanks, sewers and decentralised systems. Septic tank sludge must be collected and treated; this is faecal sludge management. Discharge standards set limits for BOD, COD, suspended solids, nutrients, pathogens and metals. They differ by country and receiving water, and permits may be stricter for sensitive areas. In Nigeria, NESREA regulates discharges; other countries have their own regulators. Check the current permit or official guideline.

keyPoints: Wastewater strength is commonly described by BOD, COD, suspended solids, nutrients and pathogens.
Primary treatment settles solids, secondary treatment uses microbes to remove dissolved organic matter, and tertiary treatment polishes effluent for nutrients, pathogens or reuse.
BOD load (kg/day) = flow (m³/day) × BOD concentration (kg/m³), and removal efficiency = (influent load − effluent load) ÷ influent load × 100%.
Sludge must be thickened, stabilised, dewatered and then safely used or disposed of.
Sanitation includes on-site systems, sewers and faecal sludge management, not only treatment plants.
Discharge and reuse standards differ by country and receiving water, so check the current permit or official guideline.

en.title: Soil and Land Degradation
en.short: Soil formation, erosion, compaction, salinisation, contamination, remediation and sustainable land use.

sections.heading: Formation and erosion
sections.text:
Soil forms slowly from parent material (the rock or sediment that soil develops from) under climate, organisms, topography and time. Soil degradation is a decline in soil quality and land capacity. Erosion is detachment and transport of soil by water or wind; it removes topsoil first. Compaction squeezes particles together, reducing pore space for air, water and roots.

The Universal Soil Loss Equation estimates average sheet and rill erosion (thin surface wash and small channels): A = R × K × LS × C × P. R is rainfall erosivity, K soil erodibility, LS slope, C cover and P support practice. For a made-up field in Kano State, Nigeria, R = 300, K = 0.03, LS = 2, C = 0.2, P = 0.5: A = 300 × 0.03 × 2 × 0.2 × 0.5 = 1.8 tonnes per hectare per year.

sections.heading: Compaction, salt and contamination
sections.text: Salinisation is the build-up of soluble salts, often after irrigation water evaporates or groundwater rises. It reduces plant water uptake. Soil contamination is harmful substances, such as heavy metals, hydrocarbons or pesticides, above safe levels. Sources include mining, industry, waste and agrochemicals. Both can make land unfit for farming or housing.

sections.heading: Remediation and planning
sections.text: Remediation means reducing or removing a soil hazard. Methods include excavation and disposal, soil washing, bioremediation with plants or microbes, and stabilisation. Choice depends on pollutant, soil and cost. Land-use planning decides suitable activities for each area. It can keep housing off contaminated or flood-prone land, protect steep slopes and set buffer zones.

sections.heading: Sustainable management and desertification
sections.text: Sustainable land management (SLM) uses practices that maintain productivity and reduce degradation, such as contour ploughing, terracing, cover crops, rotation and manure. Desertification is land degradation in dry areas, driven by drought, overgrazing, poor irrigation and vegetation loss. It is not the natural spread of deserts. A made-up case: a community in northern Nigeria plants tree lines and applies manure; this can cut wind erosion and raise yields, but success depends on rainfall and follow-up.

keyPoints: Soil forms from parent material under climate, organisms, topography and time.
Erosion removes topsoil; the Universal Soil Loss Equation is A = R × K × LS × C × P.
Compaction reduces pore space; salinisation builds soluble salts; contamination means harmful substances above safe levels.
Remediation methods include excavation, washing, bioremediation and stabilisation.
Land-use planning separates incompatible uses and protects sensitive land.
Sustainable land management and desertification control need local practices and long-term follow-up.

en.title: Solid and Hazardous Waste Management and the Circular Economy
en.short: Waste hierarchy, collection, recycling, composting, energy recovery, landfill, hazardous waste and circular economy.

sections.heading: Hierarchy and generation
sections.text: The waste hierarchy ranks options: prevent waste first, then reuse, recycle, recover energy, and dispose last. Prevention means designing products and processes so less waste arises. Generation is the amount and type of waste produced by households, commerce, industry, construction, agriculture and healthcare. It varies with income, season and industry. Collection moves waste from bins and transfer stations to treatment or disposal, and works best with segregation at source. Example: a town generates 200 tonnes a day and composts 30 tonnes, so diversion is 30 ÷ 200 = 15%.

sections.heading: Recovery and landfill
sections.text: Recycling turns separated materials such as paper, glass, metals and plastics into new products. Composting is aerobic biological breakdown of organic waste into a soil conditioner; it needs air, moisture and a suitable carbon to nitrogen balance. Energy recovery burns or digests waste to make heat, electricity or biogas, but it can create air emissions and ash. Landfill is engineered burial with a liner, leachate collection and landfill gas capture; open dumping is not sanitary landfill. Check local standards for liners and gas control.

sections.heading: Hazardous waste
sections.text: Hazardous waste is waste that is harmful to health or the environment. National rules differ, but common properties are ignitable, corrosive, reactive, toxic and infectious; radioactive waste is usually regulated separately. Classification uses lists and tests, so check the country’s regulations. Transport needs labelled, compatible containers, trained drivers and a tracking document or manifest. Treatment may be physical, chemical, biological, thermal or stabilisation. Disposal is by engineered landfill or high-temperature incineration, under permit.

sections.heading: Treaties and circular economy
sections.text: The Basel Convention controls transboundary movements of hazardous wastes and their disposal. The Rotterdam Convention applies prior informed consent to certain hazardous chemicals and pesticides in trade. The Stockholm Convention targets persistent organic pollutants. Extended producer responsibility (EPR) makes producers fund take-back and recycling of their products. The circular economy goes further: design out waste, keep materials in use, and regenerate natural systems. It contrasts with the linear take-make-dispose model.

keyPoints: The waste hierarchy is prevention, reuse, recycling, recovery and disposal, in that order of preference.
Segregation at source improves collection, recycling and composting.
Diversion rate = waste diverted ÷ total waste generated × 100%.
Composting needs air, moisture and a suitable carbon to nitrogen balance.
Hazardous waste classification, transport and disposal rules differ by country, so check national law.
Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm are international treaties on hazardous waste, chemicals and persistent organic pollutants; EPR and circular economy extend producer and design responsibility.

en.title: Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation
en.short: Greenhouse gas sources, mitigation, adaptation, vulnerability, resilience, scenarios, policy and mainstreaming.

sections.heading: Sources and mitigation
sections.text:
Greenhouse gases (GHGs) trap heat. Main sources are burning fossil fuels for energy and transport, industrial processes such as cement, agriculture including livestock and fertiliser, land-use change and waste. Mitigation means reducing emissions or increasing sinks. Options include energy efficiency, renewable electricity, fuel switching, capturing methane from landfills or oil operations, protecting forests, and changing demand. A sink absorbs more carbon than it releases, such as a growing forest.

Example: a site uses 10,000 kWh and the local grid emission factor is 0.5 kg CO2 per kWh. Emissions = 10,000 × 0.5 = 5,000 kg = 5 tonnes CO2. Check the current grid emission factor for your country.

sections.heading: Adaptation and vulnerability
sections.text: Adaptation means adjusting systems to actual or expected climate and its effects, to reduce harm or exploit opportunities. Vulnerability is the degree to which a system is exposed and sensitive to harm and lacks adaptive capacity. Exposure is who or what is in harm’s way; sensitivity is how much damage a given hazard causes; adaptive capacity is the ability to adjust. Resilience is the capacity to absorb shocks, recover and transform without losing essential functions. Adaptation examples: flood defences, drought-resistant crops, early warning, water storage, insurance and ecosystem restoration.

sections.heading: Scenarios and policy
sections.text: Climate scenarios are plausible futures used in planning. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) uses Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) for radiative forcing, meaning the extra heat-trapping energy added to the climate system, and Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) for social and economic narratives. They are not forecasts. Policy instruments include carbon pricing (taxes or permits), regulation, subsidies, public investment, information and voluntary agreements. Each has strengths and limits; carbon pricing raises revenue but may hit low-income households, so design matters.

sections.heading: Mainstreaming
sections.text: Mainstreaming means integrating climate risk and mitigation into routine planning, budgets and sector decisions rather than treating climate as a separate project. A city can add flood risk to land-use plans and transport budgets. Mitigation and adaptation can conflict, so check trade-offs. Monitoring and review keep plans honest.

keyPoints: Mitigation reduces greenhouse gas sources or increases sinks, while adaptation reduces harm from climate impacts.
Emissions can be estimated as activity data × emission factor, with units checked carefully.
Vulnerability depends on exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity.
Resilience is the capacity to absorb shocks, recover and transform without losing essential functions.
Climate scenarios such as RCPs and SSPs are plausible futures used for planning, not forecasts.
Mainstreaming integrates climate risk and mitigation into routine plans, budgets and sector decisions.

en.title: Biodiversity Conservation Management
en.short: Planning, protected areas, corridors, invasive species, restoration, community conservation, offsets and monitoring.

sections.heading: Planning and protected areas
sections.text: Biodiversity conservation management is the planned work of keeping species and ecosystems healthy. Conservation planning sets clear objectives, maps habitats and threats, and chooses actions by expected benefit and cost. It usually follows a hierarchy: avoid damage first, then minimise it, then restore, and only then compensate. A protected area is a clearly defined geographical space managed to conserve nature. The IUCN categories describe management aims, but national laws create and enforce protected areas, so rules differ by country.

sections.heading: Connectivity and restoration
sections.text: Corridors are strips or stepping stones of habitat that link patches, allowing animals and seeds to move and reducing isolation. They can spread fire, pests or invasive alien species, so they need design and monitoring. An invasive alien species is a non-native species that spreads and causes harm. Prevention, early detection and rapid control are cheaper than long control. Ecological restoration is the assisted recovery of a degraded ecosystem, with measurable goals such as plant cover or species presence.

sections.heading: Communities and offsets
sections.text: Community-based conservation involves local people in decisions, rights and benefits. It can improve compliance and local income, but it needs clear land rights, fair sharing and consent. A biodiversity offset is a measurable conservation gain that compensates for significant residual impacts after avoidance, minimisation and restoration. The aim is often no net loss or a net gain. Offset ratios vary by country and scheme. In a made-up example, a project removes 10 hectares of habitat and the agreed ratio is 2:1, so the offset area is 10 × 2 = 20 hectares.

sections.heading: Monitoring
sections.text: Monitoring is repeated measurement against a baseline and stated objectives. Good programmes use simple indicators, record methods, and compare results over time. Adaptive management uses that evidence to change actions. Monitoring should cover both the protected area and the pressures around it, such as illegal harvesting or invasive spread.

keyPoints: Conservation planning sets measurable objectives and chooses actions using biodiversity data, threats and cost.
Protected areas need clear boundaries, legal status and management; categories and laws differ by country.
Corridors help movement between habitats but must be designed and monitored for risks.
Invasive alien species are best managed by prevention and early detection before control and restoration.
Biodiversity offsets compensate residual impacts after avoidance and minimisation; offset area = lost area × offset ratio, and ratios vary by country and scheme.
Monitoring compares repeated measurements with a baseline and feeds adaptive management.

en.title: Environmental Health and Toxicology
en.short: Exposure pathways, dose-response, toxicity, risk characterisation, epidemiology basics and vulnerable groups.

sections.heading: Exposure and dose
sections.text:
Environmental health studies how hazards in air, water, soil, food and workplaces affect people. Toxicology studies harmful effects of chemicals. Exposure is contact with a hazard. Main pathways are ingestion, inhalation and dermal absorption. Exposure assessment estimates how much people take in: concentration × intake rate × duration ÷ body weight. Absorbed dose is the amount that actually enters the body.

Example: worker breathes 0.5 mg/m³ for 8 hours, inhales 1 m³/hour, weighs 70 kg. Inhaled amount = 0.5 × 1 × 8 = 4 mg. Dose = 4 ÷ 70 = 0.057 mg/kg. At 50% absorption, absorbed dose = 0.029 mg/kg.

sections.heading: Dose-response and toxicity
sections.text:
Dose-response describes how response changes with dose. Graded response measures severity in one person; quantal response counts affected people. Threshold dose is one below which no effect is expected. NOAEL is the highest dose with no observed adverse effect; LOAEL is the lowest dose with an observed adverse effect. LD50 is the dose killing 50% of test animals. Toxicity may be acute or chronic, and local (at the contact site) or systemic (whole-body). Risk characterisation combines hazard identification, dose-response, exposure assessment and uncertainty. For non-cancer effects, hazard quotient HQ = exposure dose ÷ reference dose (RfD). HQ above 1 means exposure exceeds the reference dose, not certain harm.

Example: exposure 0.02 mg/kg/day, RfD 0.005 mg/kg/day. HQ = 0.02 ÷ 0.005 = 4.

sections.heading: Risk and health protection
sections.text: Epidemiology compares disease in groups. Incidence is new cases over a period; prevalence is all existing cases. Cohort studies follow exposed and unexposed people; case-control studies compare people with and without a disease. Confounding (a third factor linked to both exposure and disease) and bias (systematic error) can mislead, so association is not proof of causation. Occupational health controls workplace exposure through elimination, substitution, engineering controls, safe systems and protective equipment. Community health looks at pollution from air, water, soil and food. Vulnerable groups include children, pregnant women, older people, workers and people with illness or low income. Exposure limits and guidelines differ by country; check the current official source.

keyPoints: Exposure pathways are ingestion, inhalation and dermal absorption; dose depends on concentration, intake rate, duration and body weight.
Dose-response relates dose to effect; NOAEL and LOAEL mark no-effect and lowest-effect doses, and LD50 is the median lethal dose.
Risk characterisation combines hazard identification, dose-response, exposure assessment and uncertainty.
For non-cancer effects, HQ = exposure dose ÷ reference dose; HQ above 1 means the reference dose is exceeded, not that harm is certain.
Epidemiology uses incidence, prevalence, cohort and case-control studies; confounding and bias mean association is not causation.
Occupational and community health protect workers and the public, especially children, pregnant women, older people and low-income groups; limits differ by country.

en.title: Risk Assessment and Industrial Safety
en.short: Hazard identification, risk matrices, HAZOP, emergency preparedness, safety management and controls.

sections.heading: Hazard identification
sections.text:
A hazard is a source of harm; risk is the chance of harm and how bad it could be. Identification asks what could go wrong, who is exposed and how. Methods include inspections, checklists, incident records, task analysis and worker interviews.

National law sets workplace duties: examples are Nigeria’s Factories Act, the UK Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and the US OSH Act. Design codes and professional registration differ by country; for example, COREN registers engineers in Nigeria. Check current regulator guidance.

sections.heading: Risk matrix
sections.text:
A risk matrix rates likelihood and severity, often on 3 to 5 levels, then multiplies or ranks them. Example: likelihood 4 (likely) and severity 3 (serious) give score 12. If the matrix sets 1-4 low, 5-9 medium and 10 or more high, then 12 is high and needs action.

Scores are a screening aid, not a precise measure. The score guides priority; it does not replace judgement. Residual risk is what remains after controls.

sections.heading: HAZOP and controls
sections.text:
A hazard and operability study (HAZOP) is a structured team review of a process design. It uses guide words such as no, more, less, reverse and other than with parameters such as flow, pressure and temperature to find deviations, causes, consequences and safeguards.

Controls follow the hierarchy: eliminate, substitute, engineering controls, administrative controls, then personal protective equipment (PPE) last. PPE protects one person and depends on correct use.

sections.heading: Emergency and management
sections.text:
Industrial safety applies these tools to workplaces. Emergency preparedness covers detection, alarm, evacuation, first aid, spill response and drills, with clear roles and contact lists. Drills should be recorded and reviewed.

A safety management system sets policy, responsibilities, training, risk assessment, incident reporting and review. It needs top management commitment and worker participation. Performance is checked by audits, near-miss reports and indicators, not only accident counts.

keyPoints: Risk score = likelihood × severity; the matrix ranks risks for priority.
Hazard identification uses inspections, records, task analysis and worker interviews.
HAZOP uses guide words such as no, more and less to find process deviations.
Controls follow the hierarchy: eliminate, substitute, engineering, administrative, then PPE.
Emergency preparedness needs alarms, evacuation routes, first aid, drills and clear roles.
A safety management system needs policy, training, incident reporting and review.

en.title: Environmental Economics and Valuation
en.short: Valuing environmental goods, cost-benefit analysis, discounting, natural capital and equity.

sections.heading: Market and non-market values
sections.text: Environmental goods are valued in two ways. Market valuation uses observed prices, such as the price of timber or fish. Non-market valuation estimates values for goods without markets, such as clean air, wildlife or a park. These values include use values, such as recreation, and non-use values, such as existence value, the value people place on knowing something exists even if they never use it. Total economic value sums them, though double counting must be avoided.

sections.heading: Valuation methods
sections.text: Revealed-preference methods infer value from behaviour. The travel cost method uses the cost of trips, including time, as a proxy for the value of a recreation site. Hedonic pricing uses differences in house prices to estimate the value of local environmental attributes, such as air quality or noise. Stated-preference methods ask people directly. Contingent valuation uses surveys to ask willingness to pay (WTP) for a change, or willingness to accept (WTA) compensation. It can value non-use values but is open to hypothetical bias.

sections.heading: Cost-benefit and discounting
sections.text: Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) compares the present value of benefits and costs. Discounting converts future values to today: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^t, where r is the discount rate and t is the number of years. A project is worthwhile if net present value (NPV) is positive. Example: costs are 1,000,000 now; benefits are 600,000 in year 1 and 600,000 in year 2; r = 10%. PV benefits = 600,000 ÷ 1.1 + 600,000 ÷ 1.21 = 1,041,322. NPV = 41,322. The discount rate matters greatly, especially for long-lived projects.

sections.heading: Natural capital and equity
sections.text: Natural capital accounting records stocks and flows of natural assets, in physical and monetary terms, using frameworks such as the UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA). Distributional issues ask who gains and who loses. A project may raise total NPV but harm a local community. Analysts should report the incidence of costs and benefits, and note that high discount rates can undervalue future generations.

keyPoints: Market valuation uses observed prices; non-market valuation estimates values for unpriced environmental goods and services.
Travel cost and hedonic pricing are revealed-preference methods; contingent valuation is a stated-preference method based on surveys.
Cost-benefit analysis accepts a project when net present value is positive: NPV = Σ (benefits_t − costs_t) ÷ (1+r)^t, summed over years t.
Discounting uses PV = FV ÷ (1+r)^t; the choice of r strongly affects long-term environmental decisions.
Natural capital accounting tracks natural asset stocks and flows, often using the UN SEEA framework.
Distributional analysis asks who bears costs and who receives benefits, not just whether total benefits exceed costs.

en.title: Environmental Policy, Regulation and Compliance
en.short: Policy tools, permits, standards, enforcement, monitoring and economic and voluntary measures.

sections.heading: Policy instruments
sections.text: Environmental policy is a government plan to protect the environment. Policy instruments are the tools that turn it into action. Regulatory instruments, often called command-and-control, set rules and penalties. Economic instruments use prices and markets: pollution taxes, effluent charges (charges on released waste), tradable permits (allowances to pollute that firms can buy and sell), subsidies and deposit-refund schemes (a deposit returned when the item is recycled). Voluntary agreements are commitments between a regulator and industry, or industry codes and certification. Information tools include public registers and eco-labels. Most countries mix these tools. The choice depends on the problem, regulator capacity and politics.

sections.heading: Permits and standards
sections.text: A permit is a licence to carry out an activity, such as discharging wastewater, subject to conditions. Conditions may limit concentration or total load, require monitoring and reporting, and set an expiry date. A standard is a rule about what is acceptable. Ambient standards limit pollution in air, water or soil. Emission standards limit what a source releases. Technology standards require a method, such as best available technique. Product standards control goods. Regulators and legal duties differ by country. In Nigeria, the National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA) sets and enforces national environmental standards, while state agencies also have roles. In Kenya, the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) is the main authority. Check the current law.

sections.heading: Enforcement and compliance
sections.text: Enforcement makes rules obeyed. It ranges from advice and warning letters to improvement notices, fines, prosecution and licence revocation. Compliance monitoring checks whether a firm meets its permit. Methods include inspections, sampling, self-reporting, audits and sensor data. A made-up case: Ada Beverages in Enugu, Nigeria, holds a wastewater permit. Quarterly sampling shows biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), a measure of organic pollution, above its limit. The state agency may require corrective action, impose a penalty or vary the permit. The firm can answer the finding and appeal under the law. Penalties and appeal rights vary by country.

keyPoints: Policy instruments include regulation, economic tools, voluntary agreements and information.
A permit is a licence with conditions, such as discharge limits and monitoring duties.
Standards may be ambient, emission, technology or product standards.
Enforcement uses a ladder from advice and notices to fines, prosecution and licence revocation.
Compliance monitoring uses inspections, sampling, self-reporting, audits and sensor data.
Regulators and legal duties differ by country, so check the current national law.

en.title: Community Engagement and Environmental Justice
en.short: Covers stakeholder analysis, participation, inclusion, local knowledge, justice and conflict resolution.

sections.heading: Stakeholders and power
sections.text: Stakeholder analysis identifies everyone affected by or interested in a decision: residents, farmers, fishers, workers, businesses, government agencies and civil society groups. For each, note interests, power, legitimacy and urgency. A power-interest grid helps: high-power, high-interest groups need close partnership; low-power groups may need support to be heard. Analysis is not a one-off list; it changes as the project moves.

sections.heading: Participation and inclusion
sections.text: Participation ranges from informing people, through consultation, to joint decision-making and community control. Arnstein’s ladder of participation describes these levels; token consultation is not empowerment. Methods include public meetings, focus groups, household surveys, participatory mapping and community advisory committees. Gender and inclusion mean asking who speaks and who is excluded. Women, youth, disabled people and minorities often carry environmental burdens but are under-represented. Use separate meetings where needed, accessible venues and local languages.

sections.heading: Justice and knowledge
sections.text: Environmental justice has three common dimensions: distributive justice (fair sharing of environmental benefits and burdens), procedural justice (meaningful voice in decisions) and recognition justice (respect for different identities and knowledge). Indigenous and local knowledge is place-based experience passed between generations. Use it with free, prior and informed consent, credit knowledge holders and combine it with scientific evidence rather than treating it as decoration. Legal consultation duties differ by country, so check national law and customary rules.

sections.heading: Resolving conflict
sections.text: Environmental conflict often arises over land, water, pollution or access. Resolve it by exploring interests behind positions. Methods include negotiation, mediation by a neutral third party, arbitration (where a third party makes a binding decision) and litigation as a last resort. Official grievance mechanisms offer a less formal channel for complaints early on. In a made-up case, a dredging plan threatens a fishing village. Fishers, the dredging firm, the local council and a women’s fish-smoking group meet. A mediator helps them agree a seasonal ban, a compensation fund and joint monitoring. The agreement is written and reviewed.

keyPoints: Stakeholder analysis records interests, power, legitimacy and urgency, and is updated as a project changes.
Participation should move beyond information sharing to consultation and shared decision-making.
Gender and inclusion require asking who is heard, who is excluded and what barriers they face.
Environmental justice combines fair distribution of burdens and benefits, meaningful procedure and recognition of identities and knowledge.
Indigenous and local knowledge should be used with consent, credited and combined with science.
Conflict is best handled by addressing interests through negotiation, mediation or formal grievance mechanisms.

en.title: Environmental Planning and Project Management
en.short: Land-use planning, SEA, project cycle, logframe, schedules, budgets, EMPs and M&E.

sections.heading: Land use and SEA
sections.text:
Land-use planning decides what may be built where and how land is protected. It uses maps, zoning, public consultation and rules set by national and local government. Laws and institutions differ by country, so check the current planning authority and local plan.

Strategic environmental assessment (SEA) is a structured check of the likely environmental effects of plans, policies and programmes before they are adopted. It should compare alternatives and feed into the plan itself. It sits above project-level assessment, which examines individual projects.

sections.heading: Project cycle and logframe
sections.text:
A project moves through identification, design, approval, implementation, and closure or evaluation. Each stage needs clear decisions and records, so that lessons can be used later.

The logical framework, or logframe, is a table linking inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact to indicators, means of verification (how evidence is checked) and assumptions. It forces clear goals and measurable results. A simple logframe can be checked by asking whether every output has an indicator and a way to verify it.

sections.heading: Schedule and budget
sections.text:
A work breakdown structure divides work into tasks. A Gantt chart shows tasks against time and dependencies. The critical path is the longest dependent sequence and sets the shortest possible duration. Budget = quantity × unit rate, plus contingency, a reserve for uncertainty.

Example: three tasks take 5, 4 and 6 days. If the 5-day and 6-day tasks run in parallel after the 4-day task, duration = 4 + 6 = 10 days. If 200 seedlings cost 500 naira each and planting labour is 40,000 naira, budget = 200 × 500 + 40,000 = 140,000 naira.

sections.heading: EMP and M&E
sections.text:
An environmental management plan (EMP) states the mitigation measures, responsible persons, timing and monitoring for a project. It turns commitments into actions that can be checked.

Monitoring checks progress against indicators. Evaluation judges relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact and sustainability. Findings should feed back into decisions, and the cycle should continue after the project closes.

keyPoints: Land-use planning controls what may be built where and must follow national and local rules.
SEA assesses plans, policies and programmes before adoption, above project-level assessment.
The project cycle runs from identification through design, implementation and evaluation.
A logframe links inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact to indicators, verification and assumptions.
Scheduling uses a work breakdown structure, Gantt chart and critical path; budget = quantity × unit rate plus contingency.
An EMP sets out mitigation, responsibility, timing and monitoring, and M&E feeds lessons back into decisions.

en.title: Professional Ethics and Practice
en.short: Codes, competence, integrity, conflicts, whistleblowing and professional registration in environmental practice.

sections.heading: Codes and competence
sections.text:
A code of conduct is a set of rules a professional body expects members to follow. It covers honesty, safety, confidentiality, respect for law and keeping skills current. Codes differ between bodies and countries.

Competence means having the knowledge, skill and experience to do a task safely. A professional should accept only work within their competence, seek advice when unsure, and sign or certify only work they have checked. Integrity means being honest and consistent, including recording data accurately, stating uncertainty and refusing bribery. Public interest means placing the health, safety and environment of the public above a client’s or employer’s convenience.

sections.heading: Conflicts and whistleblowing
sections.text: A conflict of interest exists when a personal, financial or family interest could bias professional judgement. The usual response is to disclose it early, avoid the decision if possible, or manage it openly. Whistleblowing is reporting serious wrongdoing, such as pollution, falsified results or unsafe practice, to someone who can act.
